source.title: Approximate Homomorphisms and Convergent Representations in Transducers

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper gives theoretical results about convergent structure using approximate homomorphisms between transducers, rather than measuring neural-network representations with the empirical methods discussed in the claim.
record.gate_note: The paper's own theorems and propositions bear on whether implementations of similar interfaces have shared structure, and on how that result depends on transducer class and interface metric. It does not run neural-network experiments. Empirical findings cited from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: A purely theoretical paper. It proves stability results for approximate reductions between abstract transducers (standard, linear, predictive) and measures no neural-network representations. Each version names convergence or mapping between trained models' representations, so no result bears on a version for the same kind of system. The authors frame their results as support for the Platonic Representation Hypothesis only conditionally, assuming transducers are embedded in hidden layers, and they leave empirical validation to future work.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors prove that approximate convergent structure (common minima) exists for finite-rank linear transducers and for predictive transducers under a residual metric, and fails for standard transducers. They offer this as theoretical support for the Platonic Representation Hypothesis only under the assumption that such abstractions are embedded in models' hidden layers. They call for experiments, such as stitching or probing for linear transducers, to validate it.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops theoretical transducer abstractions and approximate homomorphism results; it does not use the empirical representation-similarity methods or neural-model comparisons of the cited work.
record.method_sensitivity: The outcome depends on transducer class, interface metric (d∞, dγ, or dres), finite-rank and small-perturbation conditions for linear transducers, and support and state-separation conditions for predictive transducers.

fits_no_version.finding: Standard transducers implementing the same simple finite-rank interface need not share a common approximate-reduction minimum (no δ-minimum for δ<1, or for δ<1/2 with nearby interfaces).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In abstract transducer world models, implementations of the same dynamics need not share structure under approximate homomorphisms.

fits_no_version.finding: Minimal linear (Hankel) transducers of interfaces close to a finite-rank interface admit a 2ΓIε-linear reduction to its canonical realization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Canonical minimal linear transducer representations are stable under small perturbations of the implemented dynamics.

fits_no_version.finding: Minimal predictive transducers (ε-machines) are stable under the residual metric given state separation, but not under d∞ or dγ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Shared structure among predictive transducer implementations depends on the choice of interface metric.

fits_no_version.finding: Approximate reductions preserve the implemented interface up to O(ε) under discounted metrics, but not under the supremum metric.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The paper's approximate homomorphisms are continuous with respect to discounted interface metrics.

record.problems: The results are theoretical and concern abstract transducers, not measured neural-network representations. Their relevance to neural networks depends on the authors' assumption that such transducer abstractions are embedded in model hidden layers. The positive results require specific structural and metric conditions.

untested.parts: All: no models, no scale or capability sweep.
All: no vision or language models, no paired data.
All: no networks trained from different seeds.
All: no empirical mapping, stitching or relative representation between trained models. Stitching is only proposed as future validation.
All: no features, neurons or circuits examined.
All: no representation-similarity measure, neighbour count or input set is varied. The metrics compared are metrics on interfaces.
All: no measured alignment level, plateau, or test of shared data or objectives as causes.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's links to V4, V6 and V7 treat abstract transducer theorems as if they concerned model representations. V6's 'similarity measure' refers to representation-similarity metrics, whereas this paper's d∞, dγ and dres compare input-output behaviour. All verdict labels are therefore dropped. The paper is better catalogued as theoretical discussion (T6/discusses). It could become relevant if a later study links neural representations to these transducer abstractions.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep over model size, capability, architecture, objectives, data, or modalities.
No paired image-caption representations or vision/language models.
No comparison of neural networks trained from different seeds, features, units, or shared subspaces.
The results concern transducer reductions, not empirical mappings between neural-network representations, stitching performance, or unpaired model alignment.
No recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits are examined.
The paper compares interface metrics, but does not vary numbers of neighbours, input datasets, or out-of-distribution examples.

The paper gives conditional positive and negative results for abstract transducers, but does not test whether shared training data or objectives cause alignment, whether representations encode a common model of reality, or whether neural-model alignment plateaus.

rows.subject: standard transducers implementing the interface in Proposition 5
rows.size_stated: The interface is described as low-dimensional and finite-rank; exact rank not stated.
rows.operation_detail: Proved that exact implementations of one interface need not have a common approximate-reduction minimum.

conditions.value: the exact interface constructed in Proposition 5

rows.measure: Existence of a common δ-minimum under approximate state-map reductions
rows.value: No δ-minimum exists for every δ < 1.
rows.locator: Section 4.1, Proposition 5; Appendix A.3, proof of Proposition 5
rows.note: This is a proved counterexample for standard transducers, not a neural-network measurement.
rows.check: A proved counterexample about standard transducers, not a measurement of model representations. Links to V4 and V7 are unsupported.

rows.subject: standard transducers implementing the interface in Proposition 5
rows.size_stated: The interface is described as low-dimensional and finite-rank; exact rank not stated.
rows.operation_detail: Proved that implementations of interfaces in a neighbourhood cannot all reduce to a common transducer with sufficiently small error.
rows.measure: Existence of a common δ-minimum among approximate implementations
rows.value: For every ε ≥ 0 and every transducer C, not all implementations in the ε-neighbourhood reduce to C when δ < 1/2.
rows.locator: Section 4.1, Proposition 6; Appendix A.3, proof of Proposition 6
rows.note: The counterexample uses two exact implementations of the same interface, so they belong to every such neighbourhood.
rows.check: An abstract transducer theorem. Here d∞ is a metric on interfaces (input-output behaviour), not a representation-similarity measure, so the V6 link is wrong. V4 and V7 links are also unsupported.

rows.subject: standard transducers implementing the interface in Proposition 5
rows.size_stated: The interface is described as low-dimensional and finite-rank; exact rank not stated.
rows.operation_detail: The text states that the standard-transducer counterexample also applies to the discounted interface metric.
rows.measure: Existence of common approximate-reduction structure for nearby implementations
rows.value: The counterexample is stated to apply to dγ; a specific error threshold for this metric is not stated.
rows.note: The paper states this extension but does not give a separate numerical bound there.
rows.check: A one-sentence extension of the Prop 6 counterexample to dγ, with no bound given. It concerns abstract transducers, not neural representations.

rows.subject: canonical minimal linear transducers for finite-rank interfaces
rows.size_stated: Finite rank; dimension denoted d = rank(HI).
rows.operation_detail: Constructed a surjective linear map between canonical Hankel implementations of nearby interfaces and bounded its reduction error.

conditions.value: ε < ε(I), ensuring the selected Hankel minor remains invertible
atomic norm on the canonical Hankel row spaces

rows.measure: Error of the approximate linear reduction ΠJ→I
rows.value: Theorem 3 gives a 2ΓI ε-linear reduction from the canonical realization of J to that of I.
rows.locator: Section 4.2, Theorem 3; Appendix A.3, proof of Theorem 3
rows.note: The result applies to canonical minimal linear implementations and requires the stated finite-rank and small-neighbourhood conditions.
rows.check: A theorem on canonical Hankel linear transducers, not an empirical linear map between trained models' representations. The V4 link is unsupported.

rows.subject: contractive linear transducers related by an approximate linear reduction
rows.operation_detail: Bounded the difference between the interfaces implemented by approximately reduced transducers.
rows.measure: Finite-horizon total-variation difference and discounted interface distance
rows.value: At horizon n ≥ 1, the bound is min{1, |O|^n(n+2)ε/2}; the stated discounted bound tends to 0 as ε → 0.
rows.locator: Section 3.2, Theorem 2; Appendix A.3, proof of Theorem 2
rows.note: This establishes continuity of induced behaviour under the paper's stated contractivity and metric conditions.
rows.check: A continuity result: approximate reductions imply nearby interfaces. It is a property of the paper's definitions, not a convergence result, and it does not bear on V4 or V6.

rows.subject: standard transducers related by an approximate reduction
rows.operation_detail: Bounded the discounted distance between interfaces induced by standard transducers under an approximate reduction.
rows.locator: Section 3.1, Theorem 1; Appendix A.3, proof of Theorem 1
rows.note: The bound is for the discounted metric; the paper gives a counterexample to continuity under the supremum metric.
rows.check: A continuity bound for standard transducers (Theorem 1). It is a definitional property, not a convergence or mapping result on models.

rows.subject: minimal predictive transducers E(I) and E(J)
rows.operation_detail: Compared canonical predictive implementations of interfaces that approach one another in the supremum metric.

conditions.value: I is independent fair bits; Jn changes future outputs after the first n outputs are 0

rows.measure: Minimum approximate-reduction error from E(Jn) to E(I)
rows.value: Every such approximate reduction has δ ≥ 1/2, although d∞(I,Jn) tends to 0.
rows.locator: Section 4.3, Proposition 7; Appendix A.3, proof of Proposition 7
rows.note: The paper also states that the counterexample applies to the discounted metric.
rows.check: A counterexample for predictive transducers under d∞. It concerns abstract processes, not neural representations.

rows.subject: minimal predictive transducers E(I) and E(J)
rows.operation_detail: Compared predictive implementations using a metric on residual interfaces after conditioning on histories.
rows.measure: Error of the approximate reduction from E(J) to E(I)
rows.value: Theorem 4 gives an ε-reduction from E(J) to E(I).
rows.locator: Section 4.3, Theorem 4; Appendix A.3, proof of Theorem 4
rows.note: Unlike d∞, dres compares residual predictive laws after every positive-probability history.
rows.check: A theorem for predictive transducers under the residual metric. It concerns abstract objects, not models.

rows.subject: predictive transducers implementing interfaces J with dres(I,J) ≤ ε
rows.operation_detail: Extended the canonical predictive-transducer result to any predictive implementation by composing its reduction to E(J) with the reduction to E(I).

conditions.value: ΔI > 0 and dres(I,J) ≤ ε < min{1, ΔI/2}

rows.measure: Existence of an approximate reduction to E(I)
rows.baseline: Exact reduction from a predictive transducer to its own canonical implementation
rows.value: Every predictive transducer implementing J admits an ε-reduction to E(I).
rows.locator: Section 4.3, Corollary 2; Appendix A.3, proof of Corollary 2
rows.note: The result inherits the residual-metric and separation assumptions of Theorem 4.
rows.check: A corollary of Theorem 4 for abstract predictive transducers. It has no bearing on model representations.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Finite-rank interfaces with sufficiently small d∞ perturbations; predictive transducers sufficiently close in dres
reader_labels.reason: Canonical linear or predictive implementations admit approximate reductions under the stated conditions (R4, R8, R9).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: Standard transducers, and predictive transducers compared using d∞
reader_labels.reason: The paper proves cases with no common low-error reduction structure, including a predictive example whose interface distance tends to zero while every reduction has error at least 1/2 (R1, R2, R3, R7).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Theoretical comparisons across d∞, dγ, and dres
reader_labels.reason: The paper reports failures of closeness under d∞ (and states a predictive counterexample also applies to dγ), while giving positive bounds under discounted or residual-metric conditions (R2, R3, R5, R6, R7, R8).

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Standard transducers and predictive transducers under d∞
reader_labels.reason: The results show that approximate shared structure can fail for standard implementations and for predictive implementations under the supremum metric (R1, R2, R3, R7).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Finite-rank linear transducers and predictive transducers under the stated residual-metric assumptions
reader_labels.reason: The paper also proves approximate convergence in these restricted settings, so the negative result is not general across all transducer classes and metrics (R4, R8, R9).
